candidates.attacker_control: The request path/URL (including character case) is fully attacker-controlled. A low-privileged authenticated user can send requests whose paths differ only in case from protected paths. No special privileges are needed for the matching step itself.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked: (a) `SwitchUserFilter.createMatcher` explicitly passes `true` plus a UrlPathHelper (SwitchUserFilter.java line 566), showing case-sensitive matching is a deliberate option in some places - explicit opt-in does not justify the default; (b) RegexRequestMatcher's javadoc and code both document/implement a case-sensitive default, so the inconsistency is specific to AntPathRequestMatcher; (c) case-sensitive containers/apps reduce exploitability (attack requires case-insensitive routing); (d) the rest of AntPathRequestMatcher (MATCH_ALL handling, SubpathMatcher boundary test, method comparison, equals/hashCode) matches normal upstream structure; (e) all other sensitive controls reviewed (StrictHttpFirewall blacklists/normalization, CsrfFilter token check, remember-me constant-time signature comparison, DaoAuthenticationProvider `!matches`, session-fixation strategies, SecurityJackson2Modules deserialization whitelist, LDAP filter encoding, OAuth2 state/redirect-URI checks) appeared internally consistent.
candidates.impact: Loss of URL-based authorization/role restrictions (privilege escalation for authenticated users, or bypass of filter-chain selection) on deployments whose path routing is case-insensitive. It affects every security rule created through the default AntPathRequestMatcher constructors, not just an opt-in API.
candidates.prerequisites: Application defines URL constraints through the default AntPathRequestMatcher constructors (the default for antMatchers/antMatcher and for the login/logout processing URL matchers), and the request is ultimately routed to the same protected resource despite the case difference (case-insensitive servlet mapping or front-end/app normalization, e.g., Windows/IIS-based deployments or case-insensitive mappings). A more permissive fallback rule (e.g., `.anyRequest().authenticated()`) or a later, weaker rule must exist for the request to proceed under reduced constraints; for `http.antMatcher(...)` filter-chain selection, a non-matching chain can cause the request to be evaluated by a different (or no) security filter chain.
candidates.root_cause: In web/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/web/util/matcher/AntPathRequestMatcher.java, the two-argument constructor is documented as creating a matcher in a "case insensitive manner" (lines 78-85) but delegates with caseSensitive=true (line 87: `this(pattern, httpMethod, true);`). The one-argument constructor (line 74-76) funnels into the same path. Consequently every matcher created through these constructors performs case-sensitive comparison (SpringAntMatcher passes the flag to AntPathMatcher.setCaseSensitive, lines 288-293; SubpathMatcher lowercases paths only when !caseSensitive, lines 306-317), contradicting the documented semantics and the pattern used by the sibling RegexRequestMatcher whose code and javadoc agree. This class is the default matcher behind all `antMatchers(...)` URL authorization rules (config/.../AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry.java lines 257-265), `HttpSecurity.antMatcher(...)` (config/.../builders/HttpSecurity.java lines 1325-1327), and login/logout processing-URL matchers (FormLoginConfigurer line 249, LogoutConfigurer lines 346-353, OAuth2LoginConfigurer line 474, OpenIDLoginConfigurer line 288).
candidates.title: AntPathRequestMatcher's default constructor matches case-sensitively despite its documented case-insensitive contract, weakening URL-based authorization rules
candidates.trace: 1) Rule is built via `antMatchers("/admin/**")` -> AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry.RequestMatchers.antMatchers -> `new AntPathRequestMatcher(pattern, method)` -> two-arg constructor sets caseSensitive=true. 2) Attacker sends `GET /ADMIN/...` (or `/Admin/...`). 3) AntPathRequestMatcher.matches() -> getRequestPath() -> SpringAntMatcher.matches()/SubpathMatcher.matches() compares case-sensitively, so `/admin/**` is not matched. 4) The URL constraint intended for the resource is skipped; evaluation continues with a more permissive rule or a different filter chain. 5) If the container/app maps the differently-cased path to the same `/admin` resource (case-insensitive routing), the attacker reaches it with weaker/no role checks. The documented contract ("case insensitive manner", lines 69-70 and 79-80) states the matcher should have matched the request, indicating the delegation value `true` is the defect.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed and no tests/build could be executed (the snapshot contains no test sources). The upstream value of this constructor could not be independently compared (no git history, no external references per scope), so it is possible this differs from upstream only in my reading. Exploitation depends on the deployment routing paths case-insensitively and on the presence of a weaker fallback rule; whether this corresponds to a specific published CVE (e.g., the 5.0.12-era firewall/security-bypass advisory) is unverified.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-178 (Improper Handling of Case Sensitivity) / CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization)

coverage_summary: Scope: 1422 model-visible files (main sources only; no src/test and no docs/*.adoc present), per get_source_scope; P1 index covers all 1422 files (calls 17284, symbols 9963) with no missing files per get_relation_scope, and index facts are navigation hints only. In-depth review: web (StrictHttpFirewall/DefaultHttpFirewall/RequestWrapper/FirewalledResponse, CsrfFilter + token repositories, RequestMatcher family incl. AntPath/Regex/Mvc/IpAddress/RequestHeader, remember-me services, DefaultSavedRequest/HttpSessionRequestCache, ExceptionTranslationFilter, FilterSecurityInterceptor, session fixation/session management, security-context repository, login/logout page generation, switch-user, basic auth, X509 principal extractors, URL/header writers, some reactive server classes); core (DaoAuthenticationProvider/AbstractUserDetailsAuthenticationProvider, RememberMe/Anonymous/RunAs providers, SecurityExpressionRoot and role-prefix logic, JdbcDaoImpl/JdbcUserDetailsManager SQL paths, SecurityJackson2Modules+whitelists, SecurityContextHolder); crypto (DelegatingPasswordEncoder/PasswordEncoderFactories, BCrypt, Pbkdf2, SCrypt, LdapSha, StandardPasswordEncoder, PasswordEncoderUtils, key generators, encryptors); oauth2 client/core/jose (authorization request repository, redirect filter, login filter, OAuth2 and OIDC authentication providers, ClientRegistration, ClaimAccessor, NimbusJwtDecoderJwkSupport, JwsAlgorithms); config (WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter defaults, AbstractRequestMatcherRegistry, HttpSecurity, major configurers incl. CSRF/CORS/session/remember-me/logout/login); ldap (filter encoding and search paths); messaging; taglibs; parts of acl and cas. limitations: No test sources exist in the snapshot, so no expected-behavior or regression tests could be inspected to corroborate intended semantics.
No code was compiled or executed (explicitly out of scope), so the finding is source-level only and not runtime-confirmed.

No git history or upstream baseline is available in-run, so the code/javadoc contradiction in AntPathRequestMatcher could not be diffed against the upstream 5.0.12 source; the mapping to a specific CVE/advisory (e.g., the 5.0.x security-bypass fixed in this release window) is unverified.

The P1 relation index is syntactic/navigation-only (no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof); absence of an index record in unparsed/unsupported areas cannot be read as a clean review of those areas.

rejected_leads.lead: StrictHttpFirewall / DefaultHttpFirewall request-firewall bypass (version window would fit a security fix released in 5.0.12)
rejected_leads.reason: Reviewed both firewalls in full. StrictHttpFirewall's checks appear comprehensive for the classic mismatch classes: it rejects ';', '%3b', '%2f', '\', '%5c', '%25', '%2e' in raw contextPath/requestURI, the same decoded forms plus '%' and ';' in servletPath/pathInfo, rejects '//' and '.'/'..' segments in all four path values, and rejects non-printable-ASCII requestURIs; the encoder covers lower/upper hex variants. I could not reduce any residual bypass to a concrete, source-evident defect, so I did not submit a speculative firewall candidate. (DefaultHttpFirewall is weaker - no %2e/%5c/'%' checks - but it is the legacy, explicitly opt-in class; FilterChainProxy defaults to StrictHttpFirewall.)

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter renders the authentication exception message into HTML without escaping (line 234)
rejected_leads.reason: The unescaped append is long-standing behavior and typical AuthenticationException messages are fixed strings; I could not establish a reliable attacker-controlled path into that message in this snapshot (OAuth2 error responses are state-checked before the message is used on the error path in the provider). Left as an unconfirmed hardening observation, not the top candidate.

Present, but likely intentional/upstream (the null/null short-circuit exists to mirror legacy encoders) and not reachable through DaoAuthenticationProvider, which rejects null credentials before calling the encoder; not a source-evident exploitable bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: OidcAuthorizationCodeAuthenticationProvider does not validate the ID-token nonce and issuer (TODO gh-4442/gh-4413)
rejected_leads.reason: Documented upstream TODOs in a 5.0.x snapshot; the ID-token signature is still verified against the configured JWK set and aud/azp/exp/iat are validated. Missing hardening, but not a concrete bypass I could demonstrate from source.

summary: Spring Security 5.0.x snapshot (gradle.properties: version=5.0.12.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, Boot 2.0.8, Framework 5.0.13). Main sources only (1422 files, no tests/docs). I traced URL-authorization matching, the HTTP firewall, authentication providers, remember-me, CSRF, OAuth2/OIDC/JWT, session/context handling, crypto encoders, LDAP encoding and the config DSL. The strongest concrete defect is in the core URL matcher used by virtually every URL-based security rule: the two-argument `AntPathRequestMatcher` constructor is documented as case-insensitive but calls the three-argument constructor with `caseSensitive=true`, making security-rule matching case-sensitive. All other high-risk areas reviewed look consistent with hardening expectations; a possible firewall-related issue (the 5.0.12-era CVE window) could not be reduced to a concrete source-evident missing check.
